questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: In deriving the equation $p = \frac{1}{3}\rho\langle c^2\rangle$ in the simple kinetic theory of gases, which statement is not taken as a valid assumption? A Attractive forces between the molecules are negligible. B The volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the gas. C The duration of a collision is negligible compared with the time between collisions. D The molecules suffer negligible change of momentum on collision with the walls of the container.

stemImage.alt: Question 17: 1 =  2 p c In deriving the equation in the simple kinetic theory of gases, which 3 statement is not taken as a valid assumption?

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Recall of kinetic theory assumptions with one invalid statement to spot.
questions.misconception: Confusing elastic collisions (no KE change) with no momentum change

explanation.body:
When a molecule collides elastically with a wall, its velocity reverses, so the magnitude of its change in momentum is twice its momentum before the collision. This change is not negligible; it is what produces the pressure.

So D is not a valid assumption.

perOption.A: This is a valid kinetic theory assumption.
perOption.B: This is a valid kinetic theory assumption.
perOption.C: This is a valid kinetic theory assumption.
perOption.D: Correct. The momentum change $2mu$ per collision is what causes the pressure.

The piston is moved out until the volume of the gas doubles and the temperature falls to 25 °C. What is the new pressure of the gas in the cylinder? questions.difficultyReason: Direct ideal-gas ratio calculation with a Celsius-to-kelvin conversion.
questions.misconception: Using Celsius temperatures instead of kelvin

explanation.body:
Since $pV = nRT$, $p \propto \dfrac{T}{V}$ ($n$ and $R$ constant), so $\dfrac{p'}{p} = \left(\dfrac{T'}{T}\right)\left(\dfrac{V}{V'}\right)$.

$p' = \left(\dfrac{273.15+25}{273.15+50}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)(1.0\times10^{5}) = 4.6\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{Pa}$.

perOption.A: Does not follow from $p \propto T/V$; mishandles the temperature or volume ratio.
perOption.B: Uses Celsius temperatures instead of kelvin.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Multiplies by the volume ratio instead of dividing (treats $p \propto V$).

questions.difficultyReason: One-step use of $c_{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}$.
questions.misconception: Assuming r.m.s. speed is proportional to temperature

explanation.body: The mean translational kinetic energy satisfies $\tfrac12mc_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\tfrac32kT$, so $c_{\mathrm{rms}}^2\propto T$. Hence $T/(2T)=c_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/c_{\mathrm{rms,new}}^2$, which gives $c_{\mathrm{rms,new}}=\sqrt{2}\,c_{\mathrm{rms}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the rms speed itself as directly proportional to temperature.
perOption.C: Applies an extra factor of two after taking the square root of the temperature ratio.
perOption.D: Squares the temperature ratio instead of taking its square root.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognising that connected containers share a common pressure, then comparing V/T.
questions.misconception: Ignoring that the pressure is equal in connected containers, or mishandling the V/T ratio

explanation.body: The connected containers have the same pressure $p$ at equilibrium. Using $n=pV/(RT)$ gives $n_X=p(2V)/[R(2T)]=pV/(RT)$ and $n_Y=pV/(RT)$. The school's working therefore gives $n_X/n_Y=1.00$, even though its answer label is A.

perOption.A: Inverts the volume ratio while keeping the temperature ratio in the denominator.
perOption.B: Correct. The volume and temperature factors cancel.
perOption.C: Accounts for the doubled volume but ignores the doubled temperature.
perOption.D: Treats the amount of gas as directly proportional to temperature at fixed pressure and volume.

questions.stem:
Helium molecules have a r.m.s. speed of 1800 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ at 20 °C.

The mass of a neon molecule is five times the mass of a helium molecule.

What is the r.m.s. speed of molecules of neon at the same temperature?
questions.stemText: Helium molecules have a r.m.s. speed of 1800 m s–1 at 20 °C. The mass of a neon molecule is five times the mass of a helium molecule. What is the r.m.s. speed of molecules of neon at the same temperature? A 360 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ B 800 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ C 4000 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ D 9000 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Same temperature means same mean KE, giving $v_{rms} \propto 1/\sqrt{m}$.
questions.misconception: Forgetting the square root in $v_{rms} \propto 1/\sqrt{m}$

explanation.body: The mean kinetic energy is $\tfrac12 m c_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\tfrac32 kT$, so at the same temperature $m\propto1/c_{\mathrm{rms}}^2$. For neon, $m/(5m)=c_{\mathrm{Ne}}^2/1800^2$, giving $c_{\mathrm{Ne}}=804.98\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\approx800\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Divides the speed by five instead of dividing by the square root of five.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Makes r.m.s. speed increase with the square root of mass.
perOption.D: Makes r.m.s. speed directly proportional to mass.

Assuming the air behaves as an ideal gas, what mass of air escapes?
questions.stemText: A rigid cylinder contains 19 kg of compressed air at 9.5 times atmospheric pressure and 7 °C. It is heated to 27 °C. A safety valve releases air whenever the pressure exceeds 10 times atmospheric pressure. Assuming the air behaves as an ideal gas, what mass of air escapes? A 0.18 kg B 0.33 kg C 0.68 kg D 13.8 kg

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Ideal gas law at constant volume with changing mass and kelvin conversion.
questions.misconception: Using Celsius instead of kelvin temperatures

explanation.body: From $pV=nRT$, at fixed cylinder volume $p\propto nT$. Thus $9.5/10=n_1(273.15+7)/[n_2(273.15+27)]$, giving $n_2=0.98249n_1$. Mass is proportional to amount of gas, so $m_2=0.98249(19)=18.667\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $19-18.667\approx0.33\ \mathrm{kg}$ escapes.

perOption.A: Underestimates the loss by leaving too much gas in the cylinder for the final pressure and temperature.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overestimates the loss by leaving too little gas in the cylinder for the final pressure and temperature.
perOption.D: Uses a temperature ratio based on Celsius readings instead of absolute temperatures.

What is the average translational kinetic energy of a helium atom in the balloon?
questions.stemText: A balloon contains 2.0 moles of helium gas at a temperature of 27 ⁰C. The molar mass of helium is 4.0 g mol-1. What is the average translational kinetic energy of a helium atom in the balloon? A 5.6  $10^{-22}$ J B 6.2  $10^{-21}$ J C 30 J D 7500 J

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Single substitution into the mean KE formula after converting to kelvin; the moles and molar mass are red herrings.
questions.misconception: Using Celsius temperature or computing the total kinetic energy of the gas instead of per atom

explanation.body: The average translational kinetic energy of one helium atom is $\frac32 kT$, with $T$ in kelvin. Substituting gives $\frac32(1.38\times10^{-23})(27+273.15)=6.2\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Substitutes $27$ directly instead of converting the temperature to kelvin.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The calculation must use the Boltzmann constant to obtain the energy per atom.
perOption.D: Uses the energy of the full $2.0\ \mathrm{mol}$ of helium.

What is the $\dfrac{\text{mass of gas in P}}{\text{mass of gas in Q}}$? A $\frac{1}{9}$ B $\frac{1}{3}$ C 3 D 9

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognising equal pressure in connected flasks and combining the volume and temperature ratios.
questions.misconception: Ignoring that the connected flasks share the same pressure, or inverting the temperature dependence

explanation.body: At steady state the pressures in the two flasks are equal. The ideal gas law gives $\frac{n_PRT_P}{V_P}=\frac{n_QRT_Q}{V_Q}$. Since both flasks contain the same gas, $\frac{M_P}{M_Q}=\frac{n_P}{n_Q}=\frac{T_Q}{T_P}\frac{V_P}{V_Q}=3\times3=9$.

perOption.A: Reverses the requested mass ratio.
perOption.B: Uses only the inverse volume ratio and misses the temperature difference.
perOption.C: Accounts for only one of the two factors of three.

How many moles of gas will be transferred between the vessels when steady state is reached? A $0.18n$ B $0.21n$ C $0.82n$ D $0.86n$

questions.difficultyReason: Needs conservation of total moles with equal final pressures and kelvin temperatures.
questions.misconception: Using Celsius temperatures or assuming moles stay proportional to volume

explanation.body: Initially, the ideal gas law gives a total of $9pV/(283R)$ moles at common pressure $p$. At steady state, conservation of moles gives $p'V/(353R)+8p'V/(283R)=9pV/(283R)$, so $p'=1.022530p$. The fraction remaining in A is $1.022530(283/353)=0.819762$, so about $0.18n$ moles leave A.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Overestimates the transfer by leaving less gas in A than the final common pressure requires.
perOption.C: Reports the amount remaining in A as the amount transferred.
perOption.D: Overestimates the transfer by leaving only $0.14n$ in A.

C The volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the gas. D There are negligible forces of attraction or repulsion between molecules except during collisions.

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: The motion of the molecules is random.

options.label: C
options.text: The volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the gas.

options.label: D
options.text: There are negligible forces of attraction or repulsion between molecules except during collisions.

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct recall of the kinetic theory assumptions.
questions.misconception: Believing all gas molecules have the same speed

explanation.body: In the kinetic theory of an ideal gas, molecules move randomly with a range of speeds. The temperature fixes their mean translational kinetic energy, so equal molecular speeds are unnecessary.

perOption.A: Correct. Molecules can have different speeds.
perOption.B: Random molecular motion is an assumption of the model.
perOption.C: The model treats the molecules’ own volume as negligible compared with the gas volume.
perOption.D: The model neglects intermolecular forces between collisions.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
P and Q are two different ideal gases contained in two separate identical vessels and the masses of their molecules are $M_P$ and $M_Q$ respectively.

The ratio of their thermodynamic temperatures, $T_P$ and $T_Q$, and that of the root-mean-square speeds of their molecules, $c_P$ and $c_Q$, are

$\dfrac{T_P}{T_Q} = 2$ and $\dfrac{c_P}{c_Q} = 3$.

What is the value of $\dfrac{M_P}{M_Q}$?

A $\dfrac{1}{6}$   B $\dfrac{2}{9}$   C $\dfrac{2}{3}$   D $\dfrac{9}{2}$

stemImage.alt: Question 17: P and Q are two different ideal gases contained in two separate identical vessels and the masses of their molecules are MP and MQ respectively. The ratio of the

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: A direct ratio calculation from the mean kinetic energy formula.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to square the r.m.s. speed ratio

explanation.body:
The mean kinetic energy of a molecule is $\tfrac{1}{2}M\langle c^2\rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}kT$, so

$\dfrac{\tfrac{1}{2}M_P c_P^2}{\tfrac{1}{2}M_Q c_Q^2} = \dfrac{\tfrac{3}{2}kT_P}{\tfrac{3}{2}kT_Q}$

$\dfrac{M_P}{M_Q} = \dfrac{T_P}{T_Q} \times \dfrac{c_Q^2}{c_P^2} = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{3^2} = \dfrac{2}{9}$

perOption.A: Inverts the temperature ratio and forgets to square the speed ratio: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{3}$.
perOption.B: Correct. $M \propto T/c^2$.
perOption.C: Forgets to square the r.m.s. speed ratio.
perOption.D: Inverts the whole ratio, giving $M_Q/M_P$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A closed container is filled with ideal gas initially at a temperature of 27 $^{\mathrm{o}}$C and atmospheric pressure. It was then placed into a hot water bath maintained at 80 $^{\mathrm{o}}$C where the container achieved thermal equilibrium with the hot water bath as shown below.

When the container is opened while immersed in the hot water bath, some of the gas escapes the container.

What is the percentage of the original amount of ideal gas remaining in the container at equilibrium state?
questions.stemText: A closed container is filled with ideal gas initially at a temperature of 27 oC and atmospheric pressure. It was then placed into a hot water bath maintained at 80 oC where the container achieved thermal equilibrium with the hot water bath as shown below. 80 oC hot water bath When the container is opened while immersed in the hot water bath, some of the gas escapes the container. What is the percentage of the original amount of ideal gas remaining in the container at equilibrium state? A 15% B 34% C 66% D 85%

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires comparing gas states at equal pressure and converting both temperatures to kelvin.
questions.misconception: Reporting the fraction that escapes

explanation.body: Once released, the gas expands until it reaches atmospheric pressure, the same as its initial pressure. At that pressure the original amount of gas would occupy $V'$ at $80^\circ\mathrm{C}$, with $V/(273+27)=V'/(273+80)$ and hence $V'=(353/300)V$. The container still has volume $V$, so it retains $V/V'=300/353\approx85\%$ of the original gas.

perOption.A: Gives the percentage that escapes.
perOption.B: Uses the Celsius temperatures directly and treats $27/80$ as the remaining fraction.
perOption.C: Uses the complement of the incorrect Celsius ratio.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An ideal gas is held in a constant volume container fitted with a valve through which gas can escape.

Starting at 250 K, the temperature of the gas is raised by 1000 K while its pressure in the container is allowed to double.

What fraction of the original number of gas molecules escape through the valve?
questions.stemText: An ideal gas is held in a constant volume container fitted with a valve through which gas can escape. Starting at 250 K, the temperature of the gas is raised by 1000 K while its pressure in the container is allowed to double. What fraction of the original number of gas molecules escape through the valve? A 0.4 B 0.5 C 0.6 D 0.9

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires using the final absolute temperature and distinguishing the escaped fraction from the remaining fraction.
questions.misconception: Reporting the fraction remaining

explanation.body: Using $pV=NkT$, the initial state gives $pV=Nk(250)$ and the final state gives $2pV=N'k(1250)$. The fraction that escapes is $(N-N')/N=\left(\frac{pV}{250k}-\frac{2pV}{1250k}\right)\frac{250k}{pV}=0.6$.

perOption.A: Gives the fraction of molecules remaining in the container.
perOption.B: Results from using $1000\ \mathrm{K}$ as the final temperature instead of the temperature rise.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Would leave only one tenth of the molecules, which at five times the temperature would halve the original pressure.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: In the derivation of the relationship between the pressure, the number density of molecules and the mean square speed of the molecules of an ideal gas, which of the following is not an essential assumption?
questions.stemText: In the derivation of the relationship between the pressure, the number density of molecules and the mean square speed of the molecules of an ideal gas, which of the following is not an essential assumption? A that the number of molecules per unit volume is large B that all collisions are elastic C that there are no intermolecular forces of attraction D that the average kinetic energy of a molecule is proportional to the temperature of the gas

options.label: A
options.text: that the number of molecules per unit volume is large

options.label: C
options.text: that there are no intermolecular forces of attraction

options.label: D
options.text: that the average kinetic energy of a molecule is proportional to the temperature of the gas

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires distinguishing the mechanical assumptions behind gas pressure from a later result about temperature.
questions.misconception: Treating the temperature relation as an input to the pressure derivation

explanation.body: Gas pressure comes from momentum transferred to the walls in elastic collisions. Averaging over many freely moving molecules, with isotropic velocities, gives $p=\tfrac13(N/V)m\langle c^2\rangle$. This derivation uses molecular speeds without a temperature relation. Comparing it with $pV=NkT$ then gives the proportionality between mean kinetic energy and temperature.

perOption.A: A large molecular population in a representative volume supports the statistical average used to describe steady pressure.
perOption.B: Elastic wall collisions give the momentum change used to calculate pressure.
perOption.C: Neglecting intermolecular attraction allows the model to treat molecules as moving freely between collisions.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.difficultyReason: Students must combine the ideal-gas law with the square-root dependence of rms speed on temperature.
questions.misconception: Rms speed is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

explanation.body: For a fixed amount of ideal gas, $pV\propto T$, so $T_f/T_i=(p_fV_f)/(p_iV_i)=2\times2=4$. Since $\frac12mv_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\frac32kT$, the squared speed ratio is also 4. Hence $v_f=2v_i=2u$.

perOption.A: Assumes the temperature stays constant even though $pV$ quadruples.
perOption.B: Counts only one of the two factors of two in $pV$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Scales speed directly with temperature instead of scaling its square.

A sealed tank of gas contains a mixture of nitrogen and oxygen. The gas in the tank is at room temperature.

What is the same for the particles of nitrogen and oxygen in the tank?
questions.stemText: A sealed tank of gas contains a mixture of nitrogen and oxygen. The gas in the tank is at room temperature. What is the same for the particles of nitrogen and oxygen in the tank? A internal energy B internal energy mean square speed C mean kinetic energy D mean kinetic energy root mean square speed

options.label: D
options.text: mean kinetic energy root mean square speed

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must distinguish the temperature dependence of kinetic energy from the mass dependence of speed.
questions.misconception: Gas molecules at the same temperature have the same rms speed.

explanation.body: Both gases have the same temperature, so their molecules have the same mean translational kinetic energy, $\frac32 kT$. Since this energy is also $\frac12m\langle v^2\rangle$, the lighter nitrogen molecules have a greater mean square speed and rms speed.

perOption.A: Internal energy is a system quantity and can depend on the amount of each gas.
perOption.B: The lighter nitrogen molecules have greater mean square speed at the same temperature.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Taking the square root of the mean square speed preserves the difference between the gases.

questions.misconception: Using Celsius temperatures in the ideal-gas equation

explanation.body: From $pV=nRT$, the fixed cylinder volume and limiting pressure give $n_1RT_1=n_2RT_2$. With molar mass $M_{\mathrm r}$, this is $\frac{m_1}{M_{\mathrm r}}RT_1=\frac{m_2}{M_{\mathrm r}}RT_2$. Thus $m_2=\frac{273.15+10}{273.15+30}(15)=14.0\ \mathrm{kg}$.

questions.stemText: An ideal gas is held in a container of volume V at pressure P. The root-mean-square (r.m.s) speed of a gas molecule under these conditions is u. If the volume and pressure are now changed to 2V and 2P respectively, what will be the r.m.s speed of a molecule? A u B 2u C 2u D 4u

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Combine the ideal-gas law with the kinetic-energy relation before taking the speed ratio.
questions.misconception: Treating r.m.s. speed as proportional to the pressure–volume product.

explanation.body: The mean kinetic energy is $\tfrac12mc_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\tfrac32kT$, and the ideal-gas law gives $PV=NkT$. Combining them gives $c_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{3PV/(Nm)}$, so for a fixed amount of gas $c_{\mathrm{rms}}\propto\sqrt{PV}$. Therefore $u'/u=\sqrt{(2P)(2V)/(PV)}=2$, giving $u'=2u$.

perOption.A: Treats $PV$ as unchanged when both factors double.
perOption.B: Accounts for doubling only one of pressure and volume.
perOption.C: Correct. The pressure–volume product quadruples.
perOption.D: Scales the r.m.s. speed directly with $PV$.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires equating mean kinetic energies and taking a square root.
questions.misconception: Assuming equal temperatures imply equal r.m.s. speeds.

explanation.body: At the same temperature, the molecules have the same mean translational kinetic energy, so $\frac12 m_1c_1^2=\frac12 m_2c_2^2$. Rearranging gives $\frac{c_1}{c_2}=\sqrt{\frac{m_2}{m_1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses a direct mass ratio and omits the square root.
perOption.B: Inverts the mass ratio under the square root.
perOption.C: Equates the speeds instead of the mean kinetic energies.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Two containers X and Y are connected by a narrow tube as shown below.

[Larger container X, labelled $300\ \mathrm{K}$, is connected by a narrow horizontal tube to smaller container Y, labelled $400\ \mathrm{K}$.]

The volume of container X is twice that of container Y.
Both containers are filled with an ideal gas and the steady state is achieved with X and Y held at $300\ \mathrm{K}$ and $400\ \mathrm{K}$ respectively.

If the mass of gas in X is $m$, what is the mass of gas in Y?

A $\frac14m$
B $\frac38m$
C $\frac34m$
D $m$

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognising the common pressure and relating gas mass to volume and temperature.
questions.misconception: Assuming the volumes alone determine the mass ratio.

explanation.body: The narrow tube has negligible volume, and the containers have the same pressure at steady state. With gas mass $m'$ and molar mass $M$, $pV=nRT=(m'/M)RT$. Equating the pressures gives $\frac{m(300)}{2V}=\frac{m'_Y(400)}{V}$, so $m'_Y=\frac38m$.

perOption.A: This mass would make the pressure in Y lower than in X.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Accounts for the temperature ratio but omits the difference in volume.
perOption.D: Assumes equal pressures imply equal gas masses.
